1.   Read the following paragraph and highlight the key terms to help you answer the questions that
     follow.

      All energy forms can be separated into one of two categories: potential energy (stored energy)
      or kinetic energy (energy that moving objects have). Therefore, electrical energy (which is
      due to moving charges), light energy (which is due to the movement of electromagnetic
      waves), sound energy (due to motion of compressional waves through a medium) and heat
      energy (due to the vibration and movement of particles) are actually all forms of kinetic
      energy. What we generally call kinetic energy could be described more precisely as
      macroscopic motion energy. On the other hand, gravitational, elastic, chemical and nuclear
      energy are all forms of potential energy.

Ecology
Design an animal 19a

she The marsupial mole - a report

The Aboriginal name for the marsupial mole varies according to the locality in which it is found. In central
western Australia it is referred to as ‘the blind sand burrower’, Arra-jarra-ja, or Kakarratul for the northern
species and Itjaritjari for the southern species. Elsewhere in the southern Northern Territory, it is known as
Oorquamatia.

The marsupial mole looks like a mole or a small solid rat. It has a pouch like other marsupials, measures
about 10 - 20 cm and weighs 40 — 60 g. It has soft, fine fur of a cream-yellow colour. It has no external sign
of eyes, although there are eye spots hidden under the skin. There is also no sign of external ears, but there
are distinct ear openings beneath the fur. The nose is a small shield of horny skin used for pushing the sand
away to make a tunnel. The nostrils are small slits. The short tail, only about 2 cm long, is encircled with
rings and terminates in a tough lump. The limbs are short and powerful, each foot having five digits. The
third and fourth fingers are large and scoop-like, with sharp claws for digging. The pouch opens toward the
rear so that sand is not pushed into it.

The marsupial mole is believed not to drink, although it must eat food every day. It seems to reproduce
during early summer, but no details are known about its breeding.

EE a Read the report on the marsupial mole and sketch what you think it looks like.

b Suggest why scientists do not know about the reproduction of the marsupial mole.

¢ Predict what a marsupial mole would eat, and how it would find this food.

d_ Explain how scientists might have learnt that the marsupial mole does not drink.

Digestive system of a cow

The stomach, small intestine and large intestine of cows are similar to those found in
dogs and humans. Cows are herbivores, which means that they only eat plant material.
Plant cell walls are very difficult to digest. To help the digestive process, cows have three
extra parts to their digestive systems between the oesophagus and the stomach. These
are the rumen, reticulum and omasum. The parts of the digestive system of a cow are
shown in the diagram below,

Rumen

Cows graze, taking the food into their rumen. They can store large amounts of food in graze (v) to eat
the rumen. The rumen also contains micro-organisms that digest the fibre in the plant grass and other
material. plants

After eating, the cow rests and ruminates. Rumination involves bringing back the
chewed plant material from the rumen into the mouth. In the mouth, it is chewed again
and mixed with saliva. We call this ‘chewing the cud’. Cows can produce up to 100 litres
of saliva every day.

Because they go through the process of rumination, cows and other animals that chew
the cud are known as ruminants.

As the bacteria digest the food in the rumen, gases such as carbon dioxide and methane

are produced. Cows belch frequently to get rid of the gas.
the mouth

Reticulum and omasum

When the plant material is partly digested, it is pushed along into the reticulum. Like contract (v) to
the rumen, the reticulum is a large muscular sack containing micro-organisms. The become smaller,
muscular walls continually contract and relax, churning the partly digested food. tighten

churn (v) to mix

The food is then pushed along further to the omasum and the stomach.

PEARSON science 8


Stomach and beyond

In the stomach, the micro-organisms from the rumen are digested before the stomach
contents pass into the smail intestine. In the small intestine, the nutrients are absorbed
into the bloodstream, just as in the human digestive system.

The remaining contents of the small intestine then pass into the caecum. In the caecum
are bacteria that further digest any remaining plant material.

The large intestine is the last part of the digestive system. There, water is

reabsorbed, just as it is in the human digestive system. reabsorb (v) to

Digestive system of a dog

Dogs are carnivores. They have a simple digestive system that is adapted to meals
of meat. The digestive system of a carnivore is the shortest of all types of animals.
It is basically a long tube with a single bulge (the stomach) near the beginning.

Looking at language
Text can be written in active voice or passive voice.

In active voice the person or thing that is doing something is placed at the beginning of the clause,
because that is the main subject of the clause.

For example: The cat ate the bird.

In passive voice the person or thing that something is happening to is at the beginning of the clause,
because this is what the clause is about. And whoever is doing the action is placed towards the end of the
clause, if it is stated at all.

For example: The bird was eaten by the cat. The bird was eaten.

Genetic Variation
Label the following diagram




Humans have __ pairs of chromosomes in every cell. They exist in pairs
because you get ____ of them from your mother and half from your _______.

Egg cells and sperm cells are called gametes. Each gamete contains half of the
parents 46 chromosomes, one of each pair.

A gene is a section of DNA which codes for a specific characteristic e.g. hair
colour. Since we have two of each chromosome, we have two copies of each
gene, these are called alleles. You get one from each parent.

You can be homozygous; both alleles are the same or heterozygous where each
allele is different.

Some genes are dominant and some are recessive. A dominant gene always
expressed if present and a recessive gene only shows if there are two copies.

Your phenotype is a description of the characteristics that are shown.

Your genotype is a description of the exact combination of genes you have.

Brown hair (B) is dominant over blonde (b). If my phenotype is brown, I have
brown hair, my genotype could be Bb (heterozygous) or BB (homozygous).

Exercise 8.1
Inheritance of One Pair of Characteristics

INTRODUCTION:

From the work of Gregor Mendel and the research workers who followed him we know that the
various hereditary characteristics are controlled by genes and that these genes occur in pairs ¢.g. you
have 2 genes for type of ear lobe, 1 gene inherited from your-father and | gene from your mother.
However, reproductive cells or gametes contain the haploid chromosome number and, therefore,
only have 1 gene member of each gene pair.

Also I gene in a pair may mask the other gene. The gene that does the masking is called the
dominant gene and the masked gene is the recessive gene. Dominant genes are represented by a capital
letter and recessive genes by the corresponding lower case letter e.g. in pea plants the gene for taliness
is dominant to the gene for dwarfness, therefore, “T”’ represents the gene for taliness and “'t” the gene
for dwarfness.

Leam the following terms before continuing with this exercise.

Homozygous: the paired genes for a particular characteristic are identical e.g. TT or tt.
Heterozygous: the paired genes for a particular characteristic are different e.g. Tt.

Pure breeding organism: the paired genes are identical e.g. a pea plant with the genotype tt is pure
breeding for dwarfness.

Hybrid organism: the offspring of a cross between two parents that differ in one or more characteristics
e.g. if we cross a pure breeding tall ped plant (TT) with a pure breeding dwarf pea plant (tt) then the
offspring (Tt) is a hybrid.

Genotype: the genes carried by an organism and indicated by paired symbols e.g. the genotype of a
pure breeding tall pea plant is TT, the genotype of a hybrid tall pea plant is Tt.

Phenotype: the effect of an organism’s genotype e.g. a hybrid tall pea plant has the genotype Tt and
its phenotype is tall.

Punnett square: this is a grid system used for working out ail the possible combinations of gametes
in various crosses.

Alleles: these are the alternate forms of a gene. e.g. the alleles for height of pea plants are “T" and “t"*.

Decay (Method 1

{ Notes) Background

This investigation is a simulation of radioactive decay. Radioactive decay is a random
event. You will have noticed this by watching or listening to the uneven count rate on a
Geiger counter when it is detecting low intensity radiation. If, however, a large number of
atoms are disintegrating, the average number of disintegrations per second can be predicted
with reasonable accuracy.

The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time taken for its decay rate or activity to
decrease by one half. This is also the time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei to

underlined. The first one has been done for you. Remember that historical recounts should be
written in past tense.

People often made-up-/ make up models to explain / to explained things. Scientists perform /
performs experiments which show / shows them how something acts, or what something looks /
looked like. This information is used to develop / to develops a model. The model of the atom has
underwent / has undergone many changes.

The idea of atoms is suggested / was suggested by Democritus in ancient Greece (460 - 370 BC).
He logically deducted / deduced that matter could not continue to be cut into smaller pieces forever,
and that eventually there had to be / have to be a smallest particle, which he calls / called the atom
(about 400 BC).

In England, John Dalton (1766 - 1844) heard / heared about the experiments of other chemists.
From their results he concluded / concludes that the atoms of the same element was / were identical
and cannot be / could not _be broken. In a chemical reaction, the atoms were separated, joined or
rearranged. Dalton’s model of the atom were / was like a ball (1803).

When English scientist Joseph Thomson (1856 - 1940), and other scientists, experiment _/
experimented with electricity, they finded / found that cathode rays are / were made up of tiny
particles which travelled / travel in straight lines and carried / carryed a negative electric charge.
These cathode rays came / comed from the negative terminal (ie the cathode) and travelled to the
positive terminal (ie the anode), when very high voltages have / were applied. Thomson concludes
Zconcluded that the rays make up / were made up of electrons, which were very small (they was/
were 2000 times lighter than a hydrogen atom) and had / have a negative charge. But if negative
electrons came / come from neutral and relatively large atoms, the atom had to / has to look like a
plum pudding: the dough of the pudding was a uniform substance with a positive charge and
contained / contain tiny sultanas with a negative charge (1904).

(248 In the following text about atoms and radioactivity, there are 12 spelling mistakes. Underline the
incorrectly spelt words and write them correctly in the margin.

Radioactivity had been discovered and alpha particles were identified as tiny positive protons. A
student of Joseph Thomson, the New Zealand born Ernest Rutherford (1871 - 1937), shot a beam of
alpha particals at a very thin sheet of gold foil. He expected the protons to fly straight threw the
foil, practically uneffected by the positive and negative particles in the gold atoms. Rutherford was
suprised to find that some protons were deflected, some even bounced back to the sauce. Based on
his measurements, Rutherford concluded that the atom’s protons had to be concentrated in a small
nucleus leaving the electrons to suround it. The mass of the atom was determined by the nucleus,
which was much heavier than the electrons, and its size was determined by the electrons, which
moved around the nucleus. Rutherford’s model of an atom looked like a spherical cloud of negative
electrons with a positive nucleus in the centre. If the atom was as big as a football feild, the nucleus
would be as big as a tennis ball (1911).

The German Max Planck (1858 - 1947) formulated the quantum theory: Energy is given out or taken
in by atoms only in lots (called quanta). Niels Bohr from Denmark (1885 - 1962) concluded that
electrons jumped from one energy level to another, each jump being worth one gantum of energy.
As a result the atomic model became like a soler system: a small nucleus, containing the heavy
positive protons, was surrounded by several orbits on which the tiny negative electrons circled the
nucleus (1913).

Erwin Schrodinger (1887 - 1961) and Wolfgang Pauli (1900 - 1958), both from Austria, proposed
another model for the atom: The electron shells contained subshells of various shapes, each with a
maximum of two electrons. But it was impossible to state where a particular electron was at any
time; one could only say where an electron was most likley to be. Thus the atom appered like a
nucleus inside many electron clouds (1926).

When the English scientist James Chadwick (1891 - 1974) discovered the existance of neutrons,
which were as heavy as protons but carried no charge, the atomic model changed to include neutrons
inside the nucleus together with the protons (1932).

Ecology
Look at my tree house

12b

se Allin an ant’s day - a narrative

There once lived a small colony of ants in a nice comfortable nest under the ground, hidden by the leaf litter of a
big gum tree. They were always @ busy group going on with their day-to-day business in an orderly manner. Like any
other day, this day the ants started by receiving a message, a signal giving them the location of a new stash of food.
Many juicy mites had been located high up in their big eucalyptus tree extracting nourishing sap from new leaves.
Quickly the ants made their way out of the nest and up along the trunk of the tree.

Along their journey they met several insect borers munching away on some bark. A stick insect curiously moved
towards the ants but suddenly stopped. It camouflaged itself on the bark of the tree by staying very still, so it
looked like a leafless branch. The surprised ants suddenly understood why the stick insect interrupted its journey
when a magpie swooped down and snatched the stick insect for its breakfast. There was not much the ants could
do but to continue their journey, wondering whether the stick insect had enjoyed a last meal of fresh leaves.
Continuing their expedition, the ants noticed a young possum enjoying the sweet taste of the tree blossoms. But
the possum was rudely interrupted by a cat climbing up towards the branches, hoping to score a possum meal!
The possum hurried off, scaring the magpie away from its nest, leaving her young chicks to the fate of the cat or
the tree snake that lay absolutely still amongst the branches. ‘What an advantage it is being tiny’ thought the
ants as they continued to scurry along their path.

It wasn't long till they reached the juicy but clumsy mites. The ants skilfully surrounded the mites and together
in their gangs started to carry the mites down the tree. ‘Such strength and determination!’ thought a flying fox,
hanging upside down enjoying the fruits of the tree. It didn’t take long for a wagtail bird to notice the colourful
mites being hauled down the tree and it flew near the ants to investigate. ‘What a great meal”, and with its sharp
beak the bird grabbed and swallowed about three mites, along with the ants that had held them. The rest of the
ants took one more look at the incoming beak and decided to get out in a hurry ~ even if that meant losing the
mites. Tired and hungry, the surviving ants made their way down the tree towards their nest, only to find it was
blocked by some droppings from the flying fox.

The ants retreated into the bark of the tree, where the borers had been previously, to shield themselves from the
cold evening. Watching their nest from the safety of the tree and hoping the dung beetles would hurry up and
eat the droppings before it got too dark, the ants saw an echidna making its way towards their nest. It all
happened so frighteningly fast: the echidna found their nest, pushed its snout into the nest and with its long
sticky tongue scooped up every last ant. The ants in the tree could not help but think how lucky they were this
time and resolved never to complain again about another flying fox or its droppings! They set off together to
start another colony under another tree.

CASE STUDY:

Introduction of the
cane toad to Australia

A historical case study of the events surrounding the
release of Australia’s most hated invasive animal and

the lessons learned

The introduction of cane toads (Bufo marinus)
to Australia in the 1930s is one of the foremost
examples of an exotic animal release gone
wrong. Originally imported from Hawaii and
released in Queensland as a biological control
for beetle pests of sugar cane, the cane toad
is nowa well-established pest itself. Cane
toads currently range across Queensland, the
Northern Territory and into New South Wales
and Western Australia. Despite being less
widespread than foxes or rabbits, community
surveys consistently rank the toad as our most
hated invasive animal’ and it is listed as a key
threatening species el me Ei €

Today, ‘most eeond ion the cane
toad was deliberately released as a biological
control, but may not be familiar with the
events that led to their release.

Background: Sugar cane had been
commercially grown in Queensland since the
1860s and losses caused by white grub attacks
began to be a serious problem in the 1880s.
The grubs — the larvae of up to 13 different
species of native beetles — eat the roots of the
cane, causing the plants to die. The problem
was significant enough for the Queensland
government to bow to pressure from
canegrowers and establish the Queensland
Bureau of Sugar Experiment Stations (BSES)
in 1900. By 1935, entomologists employed
by BSES had been studying the biology of the
cane beetles and investigating solutions to
their impacts for around 25 years’.

Plenty of good science was produced during
this time — the life cycles of several beetle
species were described and an understanding
of their biology and ecology had been worked
out enabling more focused control measures.
Many field and lab trials were done in a bid to
develop effective controls including the use of
various chemical insecticides, soil-fumigation
methods, biocontrols such as parasitic fungi and

aa

Invasive Animals CRC

native insects, physical removal methods, and
agricultural and cultivation practices. Some of
these showed promise but were prohibitively
expensive or not readily available, and others
were simply not effective’.

How it happened: A government
entomologist working for BSES, Reginald
Mungomery, imported the toads, bred them
and released them‘. He was convinced
the cane toad was the answer toa major
agricultural crisis in the sugar industry, as they
had reportedly solved similar beetle problems
in Hawaii, the Philippines and Puerto Rico’.

In 1932, a paper was presented by a woman
named Raquel Dexter at the 4th Congress
of the International Society of Sugar Cane
Technologists in Peurto Rico onthe use of
Bufo marinus as a biological control for beetle
infestations in sugar crops there*. The toad
was subsequently taken from Peurto Rico
to Honolulu to control beetle infestations
in Hawaiian sugar cane fields. In June 1935,
Mungomery travelled to Hawaii where he
captured 102 toads and brought them back
to Australia. When he arrived at the Meringa
experimental farm near Gordonvale in far
north Queensland on 22 June 1935, all but one
toad had survived the journey. The toads were
housed in a purpose-built enclosure and left
to breed. On 19 August that year, 2400 toads
were released into sites around Gordonvale*.
In less than two months the number of toads
had increased at least 24-fold. Further releases
of toads in the Cairns and Innisfail areas soon
followed.

Opposition: AnotherAustralian entomologist,
Walter Froggatt, voiced concerns about the
release around this time, writing prophetically
‘this great toad, immune from enemies,
omnivorous in its habits, and breeding all
year round, may become as great a pest as
the rabbit or cactus’*®. He lobbied the federal
government to exercise caution and the

CASE STUDY: Introduction of the
cane toad to Australia

A historical case study of the events surrounding the release of Australia’s
most hated invasive animal and the lessons learned

Director-General of Health banned any further
release of toads in December 1935°. But this
ban was to be short lived. BSES and local cane
growers subsequently lobbied the Queensland
Premier and Minister for Agriculture, who in
turn pressured the Prime Minister Joseph
Lyons, who rescinded the ban in September
1936‘. Toads were then released throughout
the sugar cane regions of Queensland.

Shortfalls in risk assessment: As
reported by Griggs’, ‘all the cautious testing
characterizing the previous investigations into
cane grub control methods was completely
forgotten when it came to the cane toad.
There is no evidence of any pre-release testing
by the BSES entomologists to determine

if the toads evenate the cane beetles’.
The extremely short timeframe between
the toads arriving in Australia and the first
release supports this. The beetles that the
toads were supposed to cont rol were native
Australian species, different to those causing
problems in Hawaii and Peurto Rico, yet no
trials were carried out to see if this translated
to Australian conditions. Risk assessments of
potential harms from the introduced species
were not done.

It is not surprising that cane toads were
imported and released with apparently
little-to-no checks or control measures in
place. Colonial Australia had a rich history
of acclimatisation societies and settlers who
introduced foxes, rabbits, deer, blackberries
and other species in the 1800s, mainly for
food, hunting, or the purpose of making the
new country feel more like mother England’.
Acclimatisation societies were viewed as
scientific organisations and were the precursor
to many zoological societies that still exist
today. Quarantine was a state responsibility in
the early 1900s and mainly focused on human
health, with animal health only coming into
focus after the second World War*.

The cane toad was first recognised as a pest
in Western Australia where it was listed as
vermin under the state’s Vermin Act in 1950°.
No serious attempts were made to raise cane
toad control as a national issue until the early
1980s. The Commonwealth first took some
responsibility for the problem in 1986, with
federal funding and establishment of a cane
toad Research Management Committee".

www.feral.org.au/pe

Conclusion: There is little doubt that those
involved believed they were doing the right
thing by importing and releasing the cane
toad. Despite warnings from other scientists,
appropriate pre-release testing of potential
impacts was not done and initial control
measures were overturned in the face of
industry pressure. It is likely that the lessons
from the cane toad debacle have influenced
the strict quarantine laws and risk assessment
procedures Australia has in place today".

Ecology

To be adapted or not to be adapted

18a

All living things are suited to their living conditions. The features which enable the organisms to live in
specific conditions are called adaptations. If an organism is not adapted to its environment, it will die
there. Adaptations can be behavioural, physiological and physical (+ structural). Below is a diagram of a
grasshopper and some of its adaptations.

Behavioural adaptations

How does it behave? A grasshopper
chooses to quiver in order to mimic
the movement of leaves.

Physical adaptations

What is it like? The colour of the
grasshopper camouflages it from its
predators and its strong hind fegs
allow it to jump great distances.

Physiologica! adaptations

How is the body reacting? The
grasshopper lays many eggs and is
capable of digesting large amounts
of plant leaves and shoots.

E2@ Read the information below about the cane toad. Classify its adaptations as behavioural,

physiological or physical.

The toad was introduced to Australia to get rid of a pest. It was well adapted to the harsh
Australian climate. The toad has rough, brown, dull coloured skin giving it a perfect camouflage
against predators. The toad’s skin is also very tough with poisonous glands. This deters many
predators. Toads also have the capability of puffing up their bodies to make them look larger
and more frightening. This scares many predators away. Female cane toads lay large numbers
of eggs. They can lay them in fresh or salty water. Toads have been seen to eat a range of insects,

and even canned pet food.

Science as a human endeavour

Germination is the process of seeds sprouting and growing. For most seeds,
germination involves coming into contact with water. The seeds absorb
water, swell up and begin growing. But the seeds of some plant species (such
as wattles) germinate better after bushfires. Wattles have seeds with tough
waterproof coats. Scientists discovered that if this coating is split, water can
enter. Experiments showed that soaking wattle seeds in boiling water for a few
minutes could split the seed coat. So, for a long time, ecologists thought it was
only heat that caused wattles to germinate after a bushfire.

Focus 4.4: Reproduction

Stages of pregnancy—page 1

Skill: interpreting
Reproduction begins when sperm are ejaculated into the vagina. Once inside the vagina, the sperm move
towards the fallopian tube in search of an egg. If an egg is encountered, the sperm will surround it, but only
one will fuse with the egg and fertilise it. Fewer than one hundred sperm make it as far as the ovum or egg.
Once the egg is fertilised, the surface of the egg changes to stop any more sperm getting in. The fertilised
egg forms a zygote in the fallopian tube and begins its five-day journey to the uterus. Along the way, the
zygote divides several times to form new cells.
By the time it reaches the uterus, it has become a clump of up to 80 cells, called the morula. In
the uterus the cells continue to divide, forming a fluid-filled ball called a blastocyst. As the cells in the
blastocyst multiply, they start to move around and become different from each other. For the first eight
weeks, the developing individual is known as
an embryo.
After eight weeks the embryo becomes a foetus. The foetus is protected by a pool of amniotic fluid,
surrounded by the amniotic membrane. Oxygen and nutrients come from the placenta via the umbilical

cord.

In the urinary system, your kidneys act like a filter. Blood flows through them and is ‘cleaned’, so that useful
substances are kept in the blood, and the wastes are removed into the urine. The kidneys also make sure
that the amount and composition of your body fluids are kept at levels that are safe. Wastes removed by the
kidneys include urea formed by the breakdown of proteins, and excess salts and water. The urinary tract is
made up of the following organs that work together to produce, transport, store and excrete urine:

Activity sheet - Plants in ecosystems
The importance of plants in ecosystems

Plants are a very important part of ecosystems for a number of reasons. One reason is that
they are producers, which means they make their own food from inorganic (non-living)
ingredients, and other living things consume this food. Another important reason is that
as they are making food they take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen.

Green plants take in carbon dioxide gas through their leaves. Carbon dioxide,
water and sunlight are used during a process called photosynthesis to help the plant
produce a sugary food called glucose. When the plant breaks down water during
ohotosynthesis, one of the waste products is oxygen. The plant releases the oxygen
through its leaves. Most animals, including humans, need oxygen in the air they
breathe for respiration.

The word equation for photosynthesis is:
carbon dioxide + water (+ light energy) = glucose + oxygen

The chemical formula for carbon dioxide gas is CO, (one part carbon and two

parts oxygen).

The chemical formula for water is H,O (two parts hydrogen and one part oxygen).

All plants and animals carry out seven processes in order to stay alive. The table
below shows these seven LIFE PROCESSES.

Movement This is easier to see in animals than in plants. Plants move very slowly as
they grow.

Respiration Getting energy by reacting food with oxygen.

Sensitivity Sensing changes around them and then responding.

Growth Food is used to build up the parts of the body.

Reproduction Producing offspring (young).

Excretion Getting rid of poisonous waste chemicals from the body.

Nutrition Plants make their own food by PHOTOSYNTHESIS. Animals must feed
on plants or other animals.

Use the name MRS GREN as an easy way to remember all 7 life processes.

1    Organisms can be classified according to what they eat. One classification
     is into three groups: carnivore; omnivore and herbivore. Write the term
     that matches the definition.
                               Definition                                               Term

2    Read the description and then classify each organism as a carnivore, an
     omnivore or a herbivore.




Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2351 7   Page 1
                              Description                                          Classification

a      Bears in Canada are often photographed
       catching fish as the fish try to jump up
       waterfalls on their way to breed upstream.
       Bears are also seen picking berries from low
       bushes. Campers have to place all their food
       and rubbish in sealed containers or bears will
       steal it from them.
b      There are many different goannas and their
       diets vary. Their prey includes insects, snakes,
       smaller lizards, birds and birds’ eggs. Some
       giant goannas will kill a young kangaroo or
       even attack a dog. Goannas are attracted by
       the smell of rotting meat and feed off the
       bodies of dead animals.
c      Desert hopping mice live in very harsh
       environments with little rain. To survive they
       have to eat what is available to them and have
       a varied diet of seeds, leaves, shoots, roots
       and insects.
d      The common brushtail possum has adapted
       to living in cities and suburbs. In its natural
       habitat a brushtail possum eats mainly leaves
       and flowers. A particular favourite is fresh gum
       tips. Possums occasionally eat insects, eggs
       and meat. In urban areas they hunt through
       open compost bins to see what they can find.
e      Dugongs are large sea creatures that feed on
       sea-grass beds on the bottom of the ocean
       floor. They use their flippers to uproot the sea-
       grasses and then the dugongs chew and crush
       their food. If sea grasses are not available,
       dugongs will eat algae. Scientific studies have
       identified the remains of worms and shellfish in
       the waste produced by dugongs. Scientists are
       not sure if these are eaten accidentally with the
       sea grasses or if the dugongs eat them
       intentionally.
f      The diet of yellow-footed rock wallabies is
       similar to most other wallabies. They eat grass,
       plants and shrubs, which they chew with flat
       teeth at the back of their jaw.

CHAPTER 8: Forces, energy and motion

                                                                                                                              Worksheet 8.4



Inertia and motion
Answers
1. State Newton’s First Law of Motion.
    A body at rest will remain at rest and a body in motion will not change its speed or direction
   ............................................................................................................................................................
    unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.
   ............................................................................................................................................................
   ............................................................................................................................................................
2. Consider the following examples of forces acting on a body. In each case find the net
   (unbalanced) force and describe the resulting motion of the object. Assume north is up the page.
   (a)
                                                                                               The body will move to the left as the net
                                                                                               force is 20  10  10 N to the left (i.e.
                                                                                               west).

      (b)
                                                                                             The body will move at 45 to the right of
                                                                                             north (i.e. north-east). The net horizontal
                                                                                             force is 7  2  5 N to the right (east). The
                                                                                             net vertical force is 15  10  5 N up the
                                                                                             page (north). The net result of these two
                                                                                             equal forces is motion towards the north-
                                                                                             east.


3. A 500-kg box is placed on the tray of a utility truck but it is not secured by ropes. The ute drives
   along a highway, then the driver has to brake suddenly to avoid a wombat on the road. Use the
   concept of inertia to explain the danger to the driver.
    Inertia is a measure of a body’s resistance to a change in motion. The unsecured box is
   ............................................................................................................................................................
    travelling with the same speed as the ute. When the ute suddenly brakes, the inertia of the
   ............................................................................................................................................................
    heavy box will result in it continuing to move forward into the cabin of the ute. This could cause
   ............................................................................................................................................................
    severe injury or death to the driver.
   ............................................................................................................................................................
   ............................................................................................................................................................
4. A 1-kg pendulum is mounted on the roof of a vehicle as shown in the diagram.
                                                                                      Describe the motion of the pendulum in each
                                                                                      example.
                                                                                      (a) The vehicle accelerates from rest.
                                                                                               The bob will hang backwards towards
                                                                                               the rear of the vehicle.
                                                                                       (b) The vehicle brakes from a speed of
                                                                                           60 km/h.
                                                                                               The bob will hang forward towards the
                                                                                               front of the vehicle.

Force and gravity
Answers
Weight
1. The weight of an object is the force acting on the object in a gravitational field. The stronger the
   gravitational field, the greater the weight of a body. Weight is measured in the units of newtons
   (N)
         The weight (W) of a body of mass (m) in a gravitational field (g  acceleration due to
   gravity) is given by the formula:
                                                  W  mg
         On the Earth’s surface ‘g’ typically has a value of 9.8 m/s2 but this varies with altitude and
   latitude. On other planets, the value of ‘g’ also changes.

Newton’s Third Law
Answers
1. State Newton’s Third Law of Motion.
    All forces occur in pairs; the forces are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.
   ...........................................................................................................................................................
   ...........................................................................................................................................................
   ...........................................................................................................................................................
2. The following diagram shows a balloon rocket built by students to investigate motion. The
   balloon is mounted on a horizontal string using a length of drinking straw and masking tape.
                                                                    The inflated balloon is then released.
                                                            (a) Where along the string will the balloon be moving at
                                                                    the greatest speed?
                                                                                                 The greatest speed will occur when the balloon is
                                                                                                 initially released. This is when the force of the gas
                                                                                                 escaping is at its greatest and the reaction force
                                                                                                 acting on the balloon is at its greatest.
                                                                                    (b) Use Newton’s Third Law to explain why the balloon is
                                                                                        propelled forward along the string.
                                                                                                  The contracting rubber balloon pushes the air out
                                                                                                  of the open end of the balloon. The force of gases
                                                                                                  escaping from the balloon leads to a reaction
                                                                                                  force in which the gases push back on the
                                                                                                  balloon, which pushes it forward.
3. The photograph below shows a person pushing against a wall.
                                        The man is not moving even though he is pushing
                                        forward against the wall.
                                    (a) What is the net force acting on the man?

                                                                                    (b) If the man pushes with a force of 200 N on the wall,

                                                                                                  200 N (but in the opposite direction)

                                                                                        push back on the man?

CHAPTER 8: Forces, energy and motion

                                                                                   Worksheet 8.8



Forces, energy and
motion: Summary
Answers
Complete the statements below to compile a summary of this unit. The missing words can be found
in the word list below.
 1. Speed is a measure of the …………… rate       at which an object moves over a distance.
      Average
 2. …………… speed can be calculated by dividing the distance travelled by the time taken.
     Velocity
 3. ……………          is a measure of the rate of change in position. In order to describe the velocity
                direction
    fully, the ……………         of the change in position must be stated.
             instantaneous
 4. The ………………………                 speed of an object is its speed at a particular instant of time.
           acceleration
 5. The …………………              of an object moving in a straight line is a measure of the rate at which it
    changes speed.
 6. The average acceleration of an object can be calculated by ……………  dividing the change in its speed
    by the time taken for the change.
                                                                                       weight
 7. The force of gravitational attraction to a large object like a planet is called ……………          .
 8. An object will remain at rest, or will not change its speed or direction, unless it is acted upon
                       unbalanced
    by an outside, …………………              force.
 9. The acceleration of an object depends on the mass of the object and the ……………     total     force

RESULTANT OF TWO (OR MORE) DISPLACEMENTS

When a body is subjected to two (or more) displacements the final direct distance

travelled (unless the individual displacements are in the same direction).

“An object continues in its state of rest or uniform motion in a Straight line unless
acted on by a net external force”.

This law is also known as the law of inertia. Inertia is the tendency of a body to remain
in its state of motion.

The greater the mass of a body the greater is its inertia.

Investigating neurons
Student: ................................................................................................................... Class: ...........................................

The nervous system is made up of billions and billions of neurons. A neuron is an individual nerve
cell that transmits information around the body, combining it with information from other sources.
     Neurons have specialised functions. Some neurons specialise in transmitting information from
the sense organs and muscles to the CNS. Other neurons specialise in sending information to the
organs, muscles or glands from the CNS. Some neurons carry information between neurons.
     The number of neurons in the human body is not known. However, estimates of the number of
neurons in the human brain alone range from 10 billion to about 100 billion neurons. The entire
nervous system that extends throughout the body is comprised of neurons that connect with many
other neurons to enable the continuous communication of information around the body. Unlike skin
cells, for example, the body does not replace neurons if they die. However, the function of a neuron,
if damaged, is often taken over by another neuron.
     Not all neurons look the same. They vary in shape and size depending on where they are located
in the body and on their specific function. However, most neurons have some features in common.
     The diagrams on this worksheet show the different types of neurons in the human body. They
also shows the various parts of each neuron.

Structure of the neuron
Soma: The soma is the large section located centrally in the neuron. The soma, or cell body, is the
structure that determines whether the neuron will be activated and thus transmit (send) messages to
other neurons.
    Within the soma is the nucleus of the neuron. The nucleus contains the biochemical information
that provides the energy to keep the neuron functioning. The soma has a number of extensions that
branch from it. There are two main types of extensions — dendrites and axons. Some neurons have
thousands of dendrites that extend from the soma, but most neurons have only one axon.
    Dendrite: A dendrite is a short, thin, widely branching nerve fibre that is specialised to detect
and receive neural information. Like an antenna, dendrites receive incoming information from other
neurons and transmit the information to the soma.
    Axon: An axon is a single, tubelike, fluid-filled extension that transmits messages from the soma
to other cells in the body including other neurons, muscles, organs and glands. Most neurons have
only one axon.
    Axons vary in length, for example, some axons extend over a metre from your spine to your big
toe, others are as small as the width of a single hair.
    At the end of each axon are branches called axon terminals. Each axon terminal has a small
knob-like swelling at the tip of it called a synaptic knob or terminal button.
    The synaptic knob is a small structure like a sack that stores chemicals called neurotransmitters
that assist in the transmission of neural information from one neuron to another. Axon terminals are
located physically close to dendrites of other neurons, enabling information to pass easily between
neurons as messages are transmitted to and from the CNS.

The role of neurons
There are three main types of neurons, each of which has a different role in the nervous system. The
three types of neurons are called sensory neurons, motor neurons and interneurons.
    Sensory neurons and motor neurons are found primarily in the peripheral nervous system,
whereas interneurons are primarily found in the CNS.

   Conductors are materials that readily allow electric charges to flow through them when a
   voltage is applied across them. In the late 1800s it was discovered that it was the electrons from
   the atoms making up the conductor that moved through the material and that the protons were
   inside the nucleus and remained fixed in position.
   Metals are good conductors of electrcity and non-metals are not. An exception to this is
   graphite, a form of carbon that is a conductor. The conductivity of a metal decreases as the
   temperature of that conductor increases. This is explained by the increase in resistance to the
   flow of electrons through a conductor as it heats up. Resistance to electron flow is caused by
   vibrations of the atoms hindering the flow of electrons through a material. As the temperature
   increases the vibrations increase and so electron flow is reduced.
   Non-metals are classified as insulators. When a voltage is applied across the ends of an insulator
   almost no current flows as the electrons are not free to move through the material. If electrical
   charges are transferred to one location on an insulator, they remain there and do not move about.
   Insulators are important as they are used in electric circuits to prevent us making direct contact
   with current-carrying wires and so preventing electrocution.

CHAPTER 10: Psychology

Psychology: Summary
Answers
Fill in the gaps.
 1. affect: any experience associated with a feeling or emotion
 2. insomnia: a sleep disorder that is characterised by lack of sleep and poor quality sleep
 3. intelligence: ‘the global capacity to act purposefully, to think rationally, and to deal with the
      environment’
 4. kinesics: a form of non-verbal communication
 5. mental disorder: any disabling behavioural, cognitive or mental health problem that decreases
      a person’s level of functioning in society
 6. Prevalence: how commonly a disorder occurs in the community
 7. Psychology: the systematic study of thoughts, feelings and behaviours
 8. Behaviour therapy: a therapy that aims to change a person’s behaviour through learning
 9. Phobia: an intense and irrational fear of an object or situation that affects everyday functioning
10. Arousal: a state of physical or psychological alertness, or awareness of the environment
11. Psychopathology: the study of mental illness
12. Corpus callosum: a bridge of nerve fibres that connects the left and right hemispheres of the
      brain

Write definitions for the following terms.
1. cerebral hemispheres: the brain is divided into two halves; the left and right half or hemisphere
2. cerebral cortex: the outer layer of the cerebrum in the human brain
3. depression: a mood state often resulting in a mental disorder, usually characterised by sadness,
   hopelessness and despair
4. schizophrenia: a mental disorder characterised by a split from reality, delusions and
   hallucinations

Write a question for which the following words are the answer.
1. personality
   What is the name of the group of stable characteristics unique to an individual that determines
   a person’s thoughts, feelings and behaviour?
2. antipsychotic drug
   Which type of drug is used to treat schizophrenia by reducing the number of symptoms?
3. cognitive therapy
   Which psychological therapy deals with what we are thinking and how this affects our emotions
   and behaviour?
4. systematic desensitisation
   Which behavioural therapy is used to treat phobias by repeatedly linking relaxation with the
   feared object until the person is not afraid of it anymore?

TOPIC 11: Forensics


                                                                                                                                Worksheet 11.2



If the boot fits
Answers
Forensic scientists work together to investigate and make a deduction based on evidence provided.
You will use the photograph of the bloody footprint which is evidence in the ‘Coffee shop shoot
out’ case.

    The ability to observe every detail at a crime scene is one of the most important skills a forensic
scientist has. The evidence could be as large as the body of a victim or as small as the DNA
attached to a single strand of hair from the suspect. All of the evidence, no matter how big or small,
can be used to piece together what occurred at the crime scene.

    Imagine that you are a forensic scientist at the ‘Coffee shop shoot out’ crime scene. You have
been sent by the senior forensics scientist to investigate the bloodied footprint. Examine the
evidence and complete the
following questions.                                                                                                                                                  ©

   ...................................................
3. What is the size of the
   footprint? What size shoe could
   this be?
   Large. Size 12.
   ...................................................
4. What type of shoe has left the
   footprint? How can you tell?
   The tread mark indicates a
   ...................................................
   workboot.
   ...................................................
5. Is the footprint close to or far
   away from the source of the
   blood? How did you decide on
   your answer?
   Because of the amount of blood
   .........................................................................................
   on the tread, it could be deduced
   .........................................................................................
      that the source of blood is close.
6. Does the footprint belong to a male or female? Explain.
    Male or female. This type of shoe is worn by many people. The foot size indicates it’s most likely a male.

Extension

How can a footprint provide other evidence depending on what substance the print is left in?
Dirt or pollen embedded in the tread may be left at the crime scene. If left in soft material, such as

                                                                                                                              Worksheet 11.3



Read my lips
Answers
The study of lip prints is called celioscopy. A person’s lip prints are unique. The use of lip prints in
criminal cases is limited because the credibility of lip prints has not been firmly established in our
courts.

    The following is a case where the crime scene is a school bathroom. The crime is graffiti and
the court is the principal’s office.


      A student at the school has been writing graffiti in lipstick on the girls’
      bathroom mirror. She has been signing her work with her lip print. The
      cleaner has to clean the mirror several times every day to remove the graffiti
      and is getting tired of this prank. The principal has each of the 5 suspects
      seen leaving the restroom make her lip print on a piece of card to compare to
      the lip print on the bathroom mirror. The girls are then taken to the bathroom
      where the cleaner shows how to clean off the lipstick by using the toilet                                     Lip print found on mirror
      brush!



Your task is to compare the lip prints of the 5 suspects to the lip print found in the bathroom and
identify the culprit.

                                                                                                                             Worksheet 11.4



Mystery in the house
Answers
You are a forensic scientist within your own home. You have your forensic toolbox with you. Turn
a room of your home into a crime scene and decide the type of crime that has been committed.

    Design a crime scene investigator’s report that outlines the steps you would take to investigate
the evidence in this room.




1. How would you seal off the room?
   Close and lock doors and windows, post a look out.
   ............................................................................................................................................................
2. How would you investigate what has happened in this room before you arrived?
    Careful observation and measurement
   ............................................................................................................................................................
3. Look around the room and write down anything that is unusual, for example, a chair in the
   wrong position or a glass left on a table. How would you record this evidence?
   Photography, sketches
   ............................................................................................................................................................
4. Look for some hair and fibre evidence from the room. How would you collect and identify the
   type of hair or fibre?
   Tweezers and plastic sample bags, labelled containers
   ............................................................................................................................................................
5. Look for any objects that may have fingerprint evidence. What objects have, or could produce,
   clear fingerprint evidence? How would you collect this evidence and identify the fingerprints?
   Glass or metal surfaces, crockery, cutlery or cooking utensils, doorknobs, windows, mirrors etc.
   ............................................................................................................................................................
   ............................................................................................................................................................
6. Is there any evidence that you cannot see in the daylight? How would you identify this
   evidence?
   Ultraviolet and infra-red lighting may detect blood, fingerprints or fibres.
   ............................................................................................................................................................

CHAPTER 11: Forensics


                                                                                 Worksheet 11.5




Forensics: Summary
Answers
Fill in the gaps.
 1. evidence: anything that assists with a conclusion or judgement — that is, a testimony or
      material sample
 2. accelerant: a substance, such as petrol, that is used to start a fire or explosion
 3. database: an organised collection of data, arranged for easy and speedy retrieval
 4. analyse: examine closely to answer a question or solve a problem
 5. psychology: the science of mental processes, particularly emotional and behavioural
      characteristics. Practitioners are not medically trained and do not prescribe medicine.
 6. Botanist: a scientist who studies the life of plants
 7. Whorl: a circular type of fingerprint pattern
 8. Cuticle: the scaly outer covering of a hair
 9. Magnifying glass: a convex lens used to enlarge an object
10. Administration: the management of an organisation, business or task to meet certain goals
11. Psychiatrist: a medically trained doctor who studies the mental condition and behaviour of
      patients
12. Pollen: a fine coarse powder produced by seed plants
13. Comparison microscope: a microscope that allows two objects to be viewed at the same time
      so they can be compared
14. Liability: an obligation, responsibility, hindrance or something that causes a disadvantage
Write definitions for the following terms.
1. civil court: a law court that hears legal matters, usually minor, and not relating to a criminal
    investigation — for example, child custody battles.

2. fibres: fine threads that make up fabric and paper
3. entomologist: a scientist who studies insects
4. counterfeit: an imitation or copy that is made to deliberately deceive; for example, counterfeit
    money

5. trace evidence the tiny evidence found at crime scenes — includes hair, fibres and soil
Write a question for which the following words are the answer.
1. synchrotron
    What machine accelerates electrons to almost the speed of light and deflects them through
    magnetic fields so the electrons create an extremely bright light?

2. anthropologist
    What type of scientist studies humans — their origin and behaviour — as well as their physical,
    social and cultural developments?

3. pathologist
                                       © John Wiley & Sons Australia, Ltd
     What type of doctor specialises in interpreting test results and physical evidence found in samples
    analysed in medical laboratories, in relation to the causes of disease and other illness?

4. biased
    What do we call a person who has a preference or inclination for a partic ular line of reasoning?

CHAPTER 3: Cells

                                                                                                                                    Worksheet 3.1



History of the light
microscope
Answers
 Read the following text and answer the questions that follow.

 Before the invention of the microscope, biologists did not know
 that living things were made of cells. The first light microscopes
 were built from spectacle lenses and tubes by Zaccharias Janssen
 and his father Hans in Holland between 1590 and 1610. In 1665,
 Robert Hooke used a simple microscope that magnified by 30
 to observe thin slices of cork. He found structures that reminded
 him of the boxes or cells of a honeycomb, and so he called them
 cells.
    He examined other plant tissue in later experiments and
 observed that some of these cells contained a fluid. In the 1670s
 and 1680s Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, using a single lens
 microscope, observed cellular life forms (or protozoa) in sea
 water and rainwater. He identified microbes such as yeast and
 bacteria. His lenses were superior to those of Hooke because he
 had trained as a lens grinder and polisher. Magnifications of
 about 270 were achieved due to the great radius of curvature
 of his lenses. (The radius of curvature of a lens is a measure of
 how curved it is.)
    It was not until the middle of the nineteenth century that
 significant improvements were made to optical microscopes so
 that greater magnification and resolution could be achieved. The
 American Charles Spencer developed a company that produced
 light microscopes with magnification up to 1250. By using
 blue light, the magnification was increased to 5000.
 Throughout the twentieth century, further improvements in lens
 manufacture, improving contrast and the use of specialised dyes
 to stain tissue led to improved images of living matter.

        The structures reminded Robert Hooke of the boxes or cells of a honeycomb.
   .................................................................................................................................................................
2. Identify the first microbes that were observed using a light microscope. .............................................Yeast and bacteria
3. Identify factors that improve the magnification of a light microscope.
        Greater lens curvature; better grinding procedures; use of blue light
   .................................................................................................................................................................
4. The top figure shows a microscope used by Robert Hooke. Identify which components (A to F)
   correspond to the list below:
                       F
   Specimen: …………….…......                            Light source:D…………….… Objective lens: …………….…..                            B
   Eyepiece lens:A…………….… Mirror: …………….….........                       C                            Light focus lens:E…………….…
5. The bottom drawing shows a modern student microscope. Three components (X, Y and Z) are
   labelled. Match these letters to the letters in the Hooke microscope drawing.
     X: B           C
        …………….… Y: …………….…    F
                           Z: …………….…

Student: ........................................................................................................ Class: ...........................................................


Transpiration
1. Consider the following two diagrams of the surface of a green leaf.




      (a) Two stomates are shown. Explain why the stomatal pore at the left is open more widely than
          the one on the right.
                The stomate on the left is more open as it is actively transpiring. The other stomate is closed
                as the plant could be under water stress.
      (b) Define the term ‘transpiration’ in your own words.
                Transpiration is the loss of water from a plant through its stomates. The transpiration stream
                draws water from the roots, up the stem and into the leaves.
      (c) A student performed an experiment to measure the rate of transpiration using a bean seedling.
          She used the apparatus shown below.
                          (i) The student decided to place a thin layer of olive oil on the water surface
                              before the experiment began. Explain why she did this.
                                                To prevent evaporation from the water surface so she could see how the
                                                water level dropped due to transpiration alone
                                          (ii) Explain how the student will measure the rate of transpiration.
                                                Mark a scale on the side of the vessel. Measure the water level on this
                                                scale as a function of time.



Density of stomates
2. A student wanted to find out if there are more stomates on the top or the bottom surface of a leaf.
   She painted the bottom surface of a small section of a leaf with nail polish. When the nail polish
   was dry she peeled it off and observed it under the microscope. She could see imprints of the
   stomates in the layer of nail polish.
   (a) Explain what the student will need to do next. (Remember that she wants to find out if there
        are more stomates on the top or bottom of the leaf.) Paint the top surface of a small section of



                                                                    © John Wiley & Sons Australia, Ltd
     the leaf with nail polish. Allow to dry and peel off the nail polish; then observe under the
    microscope as before..
(b) The student decides that instead of simply counting the stomates she should measure the
    density of stomates, i.e. how many stomates there are per cm 2 of leaf. Explain why this is
    necessary. The layer of nail polish peeled off the top and bottom surfaces may have different
    areas. She needs to control this variable. By counting how many stomates there are per
    square centimetre, she is ensuring that she compares the same area for the top and bottom
    surface.
(c) The student finds that there is a much greater density of stomates on the bottom surface of the
    leaf. Suggest an explanation for this. The bottom of the leaf is usually shaded from the sun and
    so this reduces water loss from the plant and prevents wilting.

CHAPTER 4: Chemical patterns

                                                                                         Worksheet 4.2



Elements and atomic numbers
Answers
Atomic numbers and mass numbers
1. Each element is characterised by its atomic number (Z). The atoms of an element may not be
   identical, however, because elements can exist as isotopes. Isotopes have different numbers of
   neutrons and are distinguished by their mass numbers (A).
   Elements can be represented by the following notation:
                                                 Z  atomic number  number of protons
                                                 A  mass number  number of protons plus
               neutrons
   For example, the common isotope of iron has 26 protons and a mass number of 56. The number
   of neutrons is therefore: 56 – 26 = 30 neutrons.



   Complete the following table.
                                     Atomic                             Mass
     Element            Protons    number (Z)        Neutrons         number (A)        Symbol for isotope
     Magnesium (Mg)        12           12                 12              24                     Mg

     Potassium (K)         19           19                 20              39                     K

     Uranium (U)           92           92               146              238                     U

     Technetium (Tc)       43           43                 56              99                     Tc

     Beryllium (Be)         4             4                 5               9                     Be

Atomic weight of an element
2. The atomic weight of an element is sometimes referred to as its relative atomic mass. The
   atomic weight is the average or weighted mean of the isotopes of that element, taking into
   account the relative amounts of each type of isotope. Thus, atomic weights are often not whole
   numbers.
   The periodic table of the elements shows the following information for boron (B).
                      (a) How many protons are present in the boron nucleus?             5
                                                                                   10
                       (b) Boron consists of two isotopic forms: boron-10 ( 5 B) and boron-11
                            11
                           ( 5 B). Compare the number of neutrons in each isotope.
                            Boron-10: 5 neutrons
                            Boron-11: 6 neutrons
                       (c) In natural boron, which isotope of boron is more abundant? Explain.
                            The atomic weight of boron is 10.8, therefore the boron-11 isotope is
                            in the greater proportion as 10.8 is closer to 11 than 10.

CHAPTER 4: Ecosystems

                                                                                                                                           Worksheet 4.2
                                                                                                                                         Science Quest 7: pages 122–127




Food webs
Student: ................................................................................................................... Class:
.................................................................................................................................

Many animals eat more than one type of food. This means that they are in more than one food
chain. Add arrows to the diagram below to join a number of food chains together to produce a food
web. Note that some animals, such as the seagull, may actually be in more than one level,
depending on which chain you follow to the top. A food web also has decomposers. Decomposers
are organisms, such as bacteria, worms and fungi, that break down dead animals and plants. The
nutrients in the dead animals and plants are recycled back into the food web.
   Herbivores, such as the green turban snail, eat the plants and are called first-order consumers.
Carnivores, such as the dog whelk, that eat first-order consumers are known as second-order
consumers. The seagull is a third-order consumer because it eats the second-order consumer.

CHAPTER 4: Chemical patterns

                                                                                                Worksheet 4.3



Electron shells
Answers
Electron configuration
1. Complete the following table.
                                                                                                    Electron
     Atom or ion                           Proton number                Electron number           configuration
     Sodium atom (Na)                          11                                   11                  2, 8, 1
     Fluorine atom (F)                           9                                  9                   2, 7
     Carbon atom (C)                             6                                  6                   2, 4
     Calcium atom (Ca)                         20                                   20                  2, 8, 8, 2
                        –
     Chloride ion (Cl )                        17                                   18                  2, 8, 8
                   2–
     Oxide ion (O )                              8                                  10                  2, 8
                                 2+
     Magnesium ion (Mg )                       12                                   10                  2, 8
                            3+
     Aluminium ion (Al )                       13                                   10                  2, 8

Exciting the electrons
2. A student performed the experiment shown in the diagram below.
                                                    A sample of salt (sodium chloride) is placed
                                                    on the tip of a platinum wire. When the
                                                    sample is heated in a blue Bunsen flame the
                                                    flame turns yellow.
                                                    Use the theory of electron shells to explain
                                                    this observation.
                                                                      The electrons in the sodium ion absorb
                                                                      energy from the flame and move to higher
                                                                      unstable or excited shells. They then fall
                                                                      back to lower energy shells and the energy is
                                                                      released as light of various wavelengths. The
                                                                      yellow colour of the flame is the result of the
                                                                      emission of yellow light from the hot ions.


Electron shell population
3. Each electron shell is represented by a number (n) as shown in the following table.
                                      Maximum electron            The maximum electron number in each shell is

CHAPTER 4: Systems — living connections

                                                                                      Worksheet 4.4



Breathing — constructing a
report
Answers
Use the information in your textbook together with other information from the internet and library
to complete a scaffold about the topic ‘Breathing’.
Use the completed scaffold to write a final report using a word processing application. Include
labelled diagrams to show the processes of inhalation and exhalation.
 Title: Breathing
 Heading: Introduction
 Make general statements about:
    ● the name and location of the respiratory organs in the body
          lungs (in chest cavity); trachea (links nasal cavity to lung bronchi); bronchi (tubes leading
          into lungs); diaphragm (muscle to change volume of chest cavity)
     ●   the differences between inhalation and exhalation.
          Inhalation: breathing in (richer in oxygen/poorer in carbon dioxide)
          Exhaling: breathing out (less rich in oxygen/increased amounts of carbon dioxide)


 Heading: Structure of the respiratory system
 Record information about:
    ● lungs
          Two lungs; composed of many alveoli
     ●   bronchi
           Two tubes; divides into smaller tubes called bronchioles
     ●   trachea
           Tube that takes air from nasal cavity down into the bronchi. Wall has cartilage for strength.

     ●   diaphragm.
          Muscular tissue that separates chest from abdomen. Contracts and expands and adjusts
          air pressure inside chest cavity. Works with lungs to help move air in and out
 Heading: Alveoli and blood capillaries
 Record information about:
    ● the structure of alveoli
          Small air sacs (resemble bunches of grapes) at the ends of small bronchioles

     ●   the connection between alveoli and blood capillaries.
          The surface of each alveolus is covered with capillaries so that gases can be exchanged
          quickly with the bloodstream.
 Heading: Conclusion
 Make a statement about the importance of inhalation and exhalation to the health of the body.
  Inhalation brings fresh air and oxygen into the body and exhalation removes carbon dioxide waste.
  If either system is unhealthy due to smoking or disease, then the process is less efficient and
  affects the health of the whole body.

Smoking and diseases
Answers
Cancer and smoking
1. Research by the Cancer Council of NSW has shown that many deaths are directly related to the
   use of tobacco. The following 2003 data compares the percentage of deaths linked to the use of
   tobacco for some types of cancer in males and females.
  Cancer type                       Lung         Mouth/pharynx                Oesophagus               Larynx          Bladder            Kidney (pelvis)
  Male deaths (%)                     84                   57                          54                  73               43                      55
  Female deaths (%)                   77                   51                          46                  66               36                      48
     (a) Suggest a reason why the percentage of deaths in each category is lower for women than
         men.
            Women smoke less than men.
         .........................................................................................................................................................
     (b) In 2003, there were 7727 smoking-related deaths. Of these deaths, 6309 were caused by
         lung cancer. Use the tabulated information to determine whether more men or women died
         that year of lung cancer.

            .........................................................................................................................................................
            .........................................................................................................................................................
              This result is closer to the male data (84%) than the female data (77%). Thus, there must
           be more men than women in the sample.
         .........................................................................................................................................................
     (c) Use a spreadsheet application to graph the tabulated data in the form of a column graph.
         Print a hard copy of this graph when you have completed the activity.

Other deaths related to tobacco
2. Cancer is not the only disease related to the use of tobacco. The following pie chart shows the
   different types of tobacco-related deaths for Australia at the start of the twenty-first century.
                                               (a) About 20 000 Australians die each year from
                                                   tobacco-related diseases. Calculate the number
                                                   of those deaths related to:
                                                                                 (i) heart disease

                                                                                (ii) lung disease.
                                                                        (b) Explain what is meant by the term ‘passive smoking’.
                                                                                Breathing in smoke from other people who are
                                                                                smoking.


Nicotine
3. Nicotine is an addictive drug found in tobacco leaves. It is a potent nerve poison. Each cigarette
   contains about 10 mg of nicotine. Of this, about 2 mg of the drug enters the lungs in the smoke. Many
   addicted smokers may smoke 25 cigarettes a day. Calculate the mass of nicotine per day that enters:
                         25  2 = 50 mg
   (a) their lungs .....................................................................................................................................
                               25  8 = 200 mg
   (b) the environment.............................................................................................................................
